title: Seventy-eight percent on a Monday
note: Fictional unit. The 80% floor is from the PhilHealth quality circular and the AAMI standard cited in the module; your program’s procedure sets every step.
intro: You are the reprocessing technician on Monday’s morning run. Dialyzer RU-1104 belongs to Mrs. Nenita Ramos, who is due at 10:00 for its sixth use. Its baseline total cell volume (TCV) is 92 mL; today’s measured volume is 72 mL. The unit floor is 80% retained.

n1.prompt: What is the result, and what do you do?

choices.text: 78%: below the floor. It fails the volume gate; follow the discard procedure and tell the charge nurse she needs a new dialyzer.
choices.feedback: 72 ÷ 92 × 100 = 78%. Below 80% means too many fibers have closed. The charge nurse needs to know now so a new dialyzer is ready for her 10:00 session.
A repeat is legitimate only for a defined, recorded reason the procedure allows, with the first result kept. Repeating until it passes proves only that the test can be beaten.
choices.then: You find no reason for a repeat. RU-1104 fails at 78%, and you tell the charge nurse.

choices.text: Accept it for one last use: 78% is close to 80%.
choices.feedback: The floor is the floor. A dialyzer below it fails the gate, however close.
choices.then: The supervisor stops the release. RU-1104 fails at 78%, and the charge nurse is told.

n2.scene: The next dialyzer, RU-1110, measures 88 mL. Its baseline field in the record is blank. The catalog lists 95 mL for this model, which would make it 93%.

choices.feedback: A missing baseline is a hold, not a guess. Individual dialyzers of the same model differ, so a catalog value cannot stand in for this dialyzer’s own first measurement. Investigate the record by your procedure.

choices.text: Use the catalog value of 95 mL. At 93%, it passes comfortably, and the patient keeps her dialyzer.
choices.feedback: Without its own baseline there is no denominator, and the result means nothing. Hold it and investigate.
choices.then: The supervisor reverses it. RU-1110 is held while the record is investigated.

choices.text: Enter today’s 88 mL as its baseline and continue processing.
choices.feedback: That would make a used dialyzer look new and hide any fibers already lost. A baseline is measured before first use, never later.
choices.then: You stop before saving. RU-1110 is held while the record is investigated.

n3.scene: By 08:30, four of the nine dialyzers processed this morning have measured 6 to 10% lower than at their last use, which is unusual. On one, you found a loose connection on the test line and repeated the test once, as your procedure allows.

choices.text: Keep both results for the repeat with its recorded reason. Stop the run, and report a possible reprocessor fault to the biomedical technician.
choices.feedback: A legitimate repeat has a defined, recorded reason, and the first result stays in the record. Several odd results on different dialyzers suggest the equipment, not the dialyzers: report it before more are processed.
choices.then: The biomedical technician finds the volume sensor giving erratic readings, high and low.

choices.text: Keep processing, and record only the repeat results.
choices.feedback: Every result belongs in the record. And four odd results in one morning is a pattern to escalate, not to work through.
choices.then: The supervisor asks you to restore the first results and stop the run. The biomedical technician finds the volume sensor erratic.

choices.text: Finish the run so the afternoon dialyzers are ready on time, then report the odd readings to the biomedical technician at the end of the day.
choices.feedback: Reporting is right, but every dialyzer processed meanwhile is open to doubt. Stop and report now.
choices.then: The biomedical technician finds the volume sensor erratic. Five more dialyzers have been processed on it since 08:30.

n4.scene: A colleague says: “The sensor was faulty, so RU-1104’s failure doesn’t count. Retest it on the other reprocessor and release it if it passes.”

choices.text: Its failure stands; the program decides its fate. The fault puts every pass from that reprocessor in question.
choices.feedback: A later finding that the reprocessor was faulty does not erase a recorded failure. It does raise a question about every result the faulty sensor produced, passes included.

choices.text: Agree: retest it on the other reprocessor.
choices.feedback: That is the same as repeating until it passes. The failure is recorded; what happens next follows the program, not a convenient retest.
choices.then: The supervisor keeps the failure on record and refers it to the program.

choices.text: Discard it at once, so there can be no more argument.
choices.feedback: Its disposition follows the program, which may also want it kept while the fault is investigated.
choices.then: The supervisor holds it for the program’s decision.

n5.scene: Eleven dialyzers stored for release this week passed their volume test on this reprocessor since its last verified check. Three are due on the afternoon shift.

choices.text: Hold all eleven for the program’s decision, and tell the charge nurse which patients need new dialyzers this afternoon.
choices.feedback: A pass from an erratic sensor is not a pass. Hold them until they are retested on verified equipment or otherwise dispositioned, and give the floor time to prepare new dialyzers.
They passed on a sensor now known to be erratic in both directions. The result cannot be trusted.

choices.text: Hold only the three due this afternoon, and let the other eight wait in storage until the biomedical technician reports on the sensor.
choices.feedback: That protects today’s patients, but the other eight have the same doubtful result. Hold all of them for the program’s decision.

end.title: End of the day
end.text: The volume sensor is replaced and verified. The eleven held dialyzers are retested on verified equipment under the supervisor’s direction; two now fall below the floor and are discarded. Mrs. Ramos dialyzes on a new dialyzer, and the record keeps every result, every repeat with its reason, and the fault report.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Compare with the dialyzer’s own baseline; below the floor fails, however close.
  • A missing baseline is a hold, never a catalog value.
  • Repeat only for a recorded reason, and keep every result.
  • A pattern points to the equipment: stop and report.
  • A faulty reprocessor does not erase a failure, and puts every pass in question.

See Measuring against a baseline, Every gate must pass and Repeating a test.
